query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of as-deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy films are primarily governed by local microstructural heterogeneity—specifically, variations in chemical ordering and residual lattice strain introduced during film deposition—which produce a spread in the local magnetostructural transition temperatures. Reducing this heterogeneity via a controlled low‐temperature annealing treatment should homogenize the microstructure, leading to a sharper, more abrupt (and thus more hysteretic) magnetostructural transition and a correspondingly higher peak entropy change.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy films that exhibit intrinsic microstructural inhomogeneity (variations in local chemical order and residual stress) resulting from the deposition process.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled low-temperature annealing treatment (at a temperature below the ordering transition but sufficient to relieve residual stresses and promote chemical homogenization) to the as-deposited films.
generation.conditions: Perform low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles in a temperature window spanning the magnetostructural transition. Compare magnetocaloric measurements and microstructural characterizations between as-deposited and annealed samples under identical testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local chemical order and residual lattice strain—i.e. the microstructural homogeneity—which mediates the nucleation and kinetics of the magnetostructural phase change.
generation.mechanism: In the as-deposited state, heterogeneous microstructure creates a distribution of local transition temperatures, leading to a broadened (less abrupt) magnetostructural transition with moderate entropy change and reduced hysteresis. Annealing reduces these local variations, consolidating the onset of the ordered hexagonal phase and yielding a sharper (more abrupt) first-order transition that increases the peak magnetocaloric entropy change but also enhances hysteresis.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited baseline, annealed samples will display a narrower transition temperature range, a higher peak entropy change, and more pronounced hysteresis in low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
generation.baseline: As-deposited films with a microstructural distribution that yields a broadened magnetostructural transition resulting in a moderate magnetocaloric effect and relatively low hysteresis compared to bulk samples with a uniform ordered state.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be applicable to thin-film forms produced by deposition methods where microstructural heterogeneity and residual strain are inherent; the effect might differ in bulk arc-melted ingots or melt-spun ribbons where the ordering and strain states are distinct.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative changes in entropy change and hysteresis remain uncertain without preliminary experimental data. It is also possible that other intrinsic electronic or magnetoelastic effects may contribute to the magnetocaloric behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy samples: one set in the as-deposited state and a second set subjected to a controlled low-temperature annealing treatment. Perform low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles while recording temperature-dependent magnetization and calorimetric data. Concurrently, characterize the microstructure and residual strain using techniques such as TEM, XRD, and stress analysis.
measurements: Magnetization vs. Temperature curves to identify the transition sharpness
Calorimetric measurements to determine the peak entropy change
Hysteresis loop measurements during cooling and heating cycles
Microstructural and residual strain characterization (e.g., TEM, XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant narrowing of the transition range, an increased peak entropy change, and enhanced hysteresis relative to the as-deposited samples—or if no clear correlation is observed between improved microstructural homogeneity and changes in magnetocaloric properties—the hypothesis will be falsified.
